lead: A whole-body plethysmograph is a sealed box, about 600 L, in which the subject sits and breathes through a shutter. Small pressure swings in the box and at the mouth let the instrument find the gas volume in the chest by Boyle's law. That gives residual volume, the air left after a full breath out, which a spirometer cannot measure. With the shutter open, the same box estimates alveolar pressure and so airway resistance. Clinics use it for asthma, COPD and unexplained breathlessness.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.5 for lung-volume names and Chapter 2.6 for flow, pressure and airway resistance.

sections.h3: The sealed box and two pressure signals

blocks.text: The box is rigid and sealed, so the gas inside has a fixed mass. The subject sits inside and breathes through a mouthpiece. A shutter can close the mouthpiece. Two pressure transducers record the signals: one measures box pressure, P<sub>box</sub>; the other measures mouth pressure, P<sub>mouth</sub>. Box pressure swings are tiny, about 0.05 cm H2O, while mouth swings are about 10 cm H2O in the same pant. cm H2O is a pressure unit; 1 cm H2O = 98.1 Pa.

The subject pants at about 1 Hz, one cycle per second, against the closed shutter. Fast small swings keep box gas adiabatic: no heat is exchanged with the walls, so box gas follows P V<sup>γ</sup> = constant, where γ (gamma) ≈ 1.4 for air. Lung gas stays isothermal, meaning at constant temperature, because it is in close contact with blood and tissue, so it follows Boyle's law, P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>. The box pressure records how the chest volume changes; the mouth pressure records the alveolar pressure swing.

sections.h3: Thoracic gas volume and residual volume

blocks.text: With the shutter closed at the end of a quiet breath out, the lung volume is the functional residual capacity, FRC. The panting compresses and expands that trapped gas. The ratio of the two pressure swings gives the trapped volume:

blocks.where: V<sub>tg</sub> is thoracic gas volume in litres; V<sub>box</sub> is the sealed box volume in litres; ΔP<sub>box</sub> and ΔP<sub>mouth</sub> are the peak-to-peak pressure swings in the same pressure unit, usually cm H2O. The exact relation carries the adiabatic factor for box gas, about 1.4: V<sub>tg</sub> ≈ V<sub>box</sub> × ΔP<sub>box</sub>/(1.4 × ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>).

blocks.text: Using the exam approximation, a 600 L box with a 0.05 cm H2O box swing and a 10 cm H2O mouth swing gives V<sub>tg</sub> = 600 × 0.05/10 = 3.0 L. At that moment V<sub>tg</sub> equals FRC. A spirometer can measure expiratory reserve volume, ERV, the extra air pushed out after a quiet breath out, and vital capacity, VC, the largest breath. It cannot measure what stays inside. Subtract:
RV = FRC − ERV;  TLC = RV + VC
blocks.where: RV is residual volume; FRC is functional residual capacity, equal to V<sub>tg</sub> when the shutter closes at end-expiration; ERV is expiratory reserve volume; TLC is total lung capacity; VC is vital capacity. All volumes in litres.

blocks.text: Residual volume is the air left after a full forced breath out; total lung capacity is the sum of residual volume and vital capacity. Lung gas is reported at BTPS: body temperature, ambient pressure, saturated with water vapour. At 37°C water vapour pressure is 47 mmHg. If a question gives barometric pressure P<sub>B</sub>, the full Boyle's-law correction is V<sub>tg</sub> × (P<sub>B</sub> − 47)/P<sub>B</sub>; at P<sub>B</sub> = 760 mmHg the factor is about 0.938. Exam sums often use the simple ratio, as in the worked example.

sections.h3: Airway resistance with the shutter open

blocks.text: The shutter opens. The subject breathes through a pneumotachometer, which measures airflow from a small pressure drop across a known resistance. Alveolar pressure cannot be measured directly, so the box pressure is used as a surrogate. A calibration factor k converts box pressure swing to alveolar pressure: P<sub>A</sub> = k × ΔP<sub>box</sub>. The factor is found with a known resistance or a mouth pressure reference.
Airway resistance is the pressure difference from alveolus to mouth divided by flow:

blocks.where: R<sub>aw</sub> is airway resistance in cm H2O per L/s; P<sub>A</sub> is alveolar pressure in cm H2O; P<sub>mouth</sub> is mouth pressure in cm H2O; V̇ (V-dot) is airflow in L/s.

blocks.text: A flow of 2 L/s with a 4 cm H2O alveolar-to-mouth difference gives R<sub>aw</sub> = 4/2 = 2 cm H2O per L/s. Normal airway resistance is roughly 0.6 to 2.4 cm H2O per L/s. Values above this suggest obstruction. Conductance is 1/R<sub>aw</sub>. Specific airway conductance divides conductance by V<sub>tg</sub>, so it is less dependent on lung size; only a few universities ask for it. Units matter: write cm H2O per L/s, not cm H2O/L.

figure.caption: Panting against a closed shutter gives a tiny box-pressure swing and a larger mouth-pressure swing. Their ratio, scaled by the 600 L box, gives thoracic gas volume 3.0 L and residual volume 1.8 L.

spec.title: Plethysmograph measurement
spec.aria: A subject in a sealed 600 L box pants against a closed shutter; box pressure 0.05 cm H2O and mouth pressure 10 cm H2O give thoracic gas volume 3.0 L, and subtracting expiratory reserve volume 1.2 L gives residual volume 1.8 L.

examples.question: A subject sits in a 600 L plethysmograph. With the shutter closed he pants; mouth pressure swings by 10 cm H2O and box pressure by 0.05 cm H2O. (a) Find the thoracic gas volume. (b) His expiratory reserve volume is 1.2 L and slow vital capacity is 4.0 L; find residual volume and total lung capacity. (c) With the shutter open, a flow of 2 L/s gives a box pressure swing equal to 4 cm H2O of alveolar pressure; find airway resistance.
steps: Write the closed-shutter exam approximation: V<sub>tg</sub> = V<sub>box</sub> × ΔP<sub>box</sub>/ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>. Put V<sub>box</sub> = 600 L, ΔP<sub>box</sub> = 0.05 cm H2O, ΔP<sub>mouth</sub> = 10 cm H2O.
V<sub>tg</sub> = 600 × 0.05/10 = 600 × 0.005 = 3.0 L. This is FRC because the shutter was closed at end-expiration.
Total lung capacity = RV + VC = 1.8 + 4.0 = 5.8 L.

Airway resistance = pressure difference / flow = 4/2 = 2.0 cm H2O per L/s. This is within the normal range of about 0.6 to 2.4 cm H2O per L/s, toward its upper end. Obstruction is suggested only when R<sub>aw</sub> rises above about 2.4 cm H2O per L/s.
examples.answer: V<sub>tg</sub> = 3.0 L (FRC), residual volume = 1.8 L, total lung capacity = 5.8 L, and airway resistance = 2.0 cm H2O per L/s, within the normal range toward its upper end; obstruction is suggested only above about 2.4 cm H2O per L/s.
examples.check:
V_box = 600
dP_box = 0.05
dP_mouth = 10
V_tg = V_box * dP_box / dP_mouth
ERV = 1.2
RV = V_tg - ERV
VC = 4.0
TLC = RV + VC
P_alv = 4.0
flow = 2.0
R_aw = P_alv / flow
print(round(V_tg, 1))
print(round(RV, 1))
print(round(TLC, 1))
print(round(R_aw, 1))

traps: Treating ΔP<sub>box</sub> as ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>: box swings are about 0.05 cm H2O, mouth swings about 10 cm H2O; the ratio has no units and must be applied to V<sub>box</sub>.
Forgetting BTPS and water vapour: lung gas is at body temperature, pressure and saturation; subtract 47 mmHg water vapour pressure before using Boyle's law if the question gives barometric pressure.
Mixing FRC and residual volume: V<sub>tg</sub> at shutter closure is FRC, not residual volume; residual volume = FRC − ERV.
Using airway-resistance units as cm H2O/L instead of cm H2O per L/s.
Assuming box pressure is alveolar pressure in open-shutter resistance: use the calibration factor between box pressure and alveolar pressure.

quiz.q: What does a whole-body plethysmograph measure when the shutter is closed?
quiz.a: It measures thoracic gas volume at the current lung volume, usually FRC, from Boyle's law using box and mouth pressure swings.

quiz.q: Why is lung gas treated as isothermal but box gas as adiabatic during panting?
quiz.a: Lung gas exchanges heat with blood and tissue and has a large surface, so its compression is near isothermal. Box gas has little time and small surface for heat exchange during about 1 Hz panting, so its compression is near adiabatic.

quiz.q: A 500 L box gives ΔP<sub>box</sub> = 0.06 cm H2O for ΔP<sub>mouth</sub> = 12 cm H2O. Find V<sub>tg</sub>.
V<sub>tg</sub> = 3.5 L, ERV = 1.1 L, VC = 4.2 L. Find RV and TLC.
A patient has normal VC but a high RV/TLC ratio. Which measurement did spirometry miss and how does plethysmography catch it?
quiz.a: Spirometry misses RV because RV cannot be exhaled. Plethysmography measures FRC as V<sub>tg</sub>, subtracts ERV to get RV, so it shows hyperinflation when RV/TLC is high.

quiz.q: Flow is 1.5 L/s and the alveolar-to-mouth pressure difference is 3 cm H2O. Find airway resistance.
Why can box pressure be used for airway resistance only after a calibration factor, while mouth pressure is used directly?
quiz.a: Box pressure is a surrogate for alveolar pressure; it depends on box volume, gas compression and subject movement. A calibration relates box swing to alveolar pressure. Mouth pressure is measured at the mouth, so the pressure difference is direct.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern body plethysmographs add a slow vital-capacity manoeuvre in the same sitting, and some use oscillometry to check resistance without panting. Research uses the same box for lung-volume measurement in children and for tracking airway obstruction in cystic fibrosis. Newer curricula push specific airway conductance and BTPS correction because they matter in clinical reports.
